activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Lines of latitude are also called parallels because they never meet, and lines of longitude are called meridians.
story:
Brayden slid down the bench at Gate 14 and unfolded the battered atlas his grandpa had shoved into his backpack that morning. "For the layover," Grandpa had said. "Find me." His flight was going to a city Brayden had never heard of, and all he had was a scribbled note: 41 N, 29 E.

The note had made sense for about two seconds. Then Brayden had opened the atlas and found the whole world crisscrossed with thin lines, dozens of them, horizontal and vertical, like a cage built by a very tidy rodent with a ruler. He ran his finger along one line near the top of the page, then along its neighbor. They ran side by side across the whole map and never, ever touched.

He flashed back to Sunday, when he'd flopped onto Grandpa's couch and paged through this same atlas out of boredom. Laurianne had been there, because her mom had come over to help sort boxes. "Those sideways ones," Laurianne had said, tapping the page, "are called parallels because they never meet. The up-and-down ones are meridians." Brayden had made his hands mimic two trains running side by side, never crashing, and Grandpa had laughed so hard he'd spilled his tea. Parallel lines, sideways. Meridians, up and down. He had thought it was just a goofy fact. Now it was a treasure map.

So 41 had to be counted along a parallel, starting from zero at the equator. He traced upward, mouthing the numbers, then swept his finger east along the parallel until it crossed a meridian marked 29. He tapped the spot. Istanbul. "Found you," he whispered, and did a small but vigorous fist pump that made a woman across the aisle glance over.

Faye from his class plopped down beside him, waiting for her own grandfather. "Whatcha doing?"

"Finding my grandpa. Secret code. Lat and long."

Faye squinted at the map. "That's not where the board says his plane is going."

Brayden checked the departures screen. The gate had changed, and the destination read Athens, not Istanbul at all. He looked from the screen to his note, then back.

"Grandpa," he muttered, "you gave me the wrong city on purpose."

He found a fresh line for 37 N, 23 E, and started counting.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
"I think most students at our school walk," Hallie said, leaning over the lab table. "That's why the bike racks are always empty."

"That's just an opinion," Tamara said. "You can't know that by looking at bike racks."

Mr. Kang rapped a knuckle on the whiteboard. "Settle down, everyone. Your homework is one paragraph on a claim you could actually check."

Brooke frowned at her notebook. A claim you could check. Hallie's sentence spun in her head. Most students at our school walk to school. Was that an opinion, or was it something you could check, even though nobody had checked it yet?

"You could count," she said slowly. "You could ask everybody how they get here."

Hallie sat up. "A survey."

"Nobody's done it," Tamara pointed out.

"So what?" Brooke said. "It could still be checked. That's the difference."

The next morning, Mr. Kang let them run the survey during homeroom. He was careful, though, and didn't explain anything; he simply handed Brooke the clipboard and said the rest was hers. "Delegate the rooms," he suggested. "You can't cover the whole school alone."

So Brooke delegated. Tamara took the sixth-grade hallway, Hallie took the gym, where the coach let her stand by the door with her clipboard. It caused a small controversy in the cafeteria when a boy from the seventh grade insisted the survey was pointless because "everyone obviously takes the bus," and he got a bit aggressive about it, waving his tray until his friend pulled him back down into his seat.

By lunch they had tallied every class. Bus: 289. Walk: 96. Car: 144.

Hallie stared at the numbers. "I was completely wrong."

"You were checkably wrong," Brooke said. "That's better."

Tamara laughed so hard milk came out of her nose, and Hallie, still holding the clipboard, began counting the tallies again, one by one, as if the marks might rearrange themselves.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A standard AA battery provides about 1.5 volts.
story:
Zachary crouched on the patio with a battery, a bulb, three wires, and a little metal switch he had pried from a broken flashlight. The bulb had to light by four o'clock, because his little sister's birthday was tomorrow and he wanted the circuit hidden inside her cardboard castle. So far the bulb did nothing. He flipped the switch up, down, up again, and stared at the dark glass as if staring hard enough would mediate between the battery and the bulb.

Louisa dropped her bike on the grass and came over. "You wired it wrong," she said.

"I wired it fine. I think." Zachary lifted one wire and followed it with his finger. "It goes from the battery to the switch, then to the bulb, then back to the battery. Like a circle."

Louisa tilted her head. "Then why is it dark?"

He traced the circle again, slower. The wires he could see were fine, which meant the problem was somewhere he could not see, inside something. He unscrewed the bulb and held it up to the sun. The thin wire inside was broken. "It's not the circuit," he said. "It's the bulb." He ran inside, dug through the junk drawer, and came back with a fat flashlight bulb and a holder for it.

The new bulb glowed, but weakly, an orange ember instead of the bright beam he wanted for the castle windows. Cashton leaned over the fence from next door. "That's sad," he said.

"It's one battery," Louisa said. She turned it over and read the side. "A standard AA battery provides about one point five volts. That's all you're getting."

Zachary counted on his fingers. Two batteries would double it, three would more. He taped three AAs together end to end, wired them in, and flipped the switch. The bulb blazed, white and steady, and all three of them threw their hands up like the castle had already won a prize. Cashton changed his mind about helping and climbed over the fence, holding out a roll of tape.

"Best windows in the kingdom," he said.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: The prime meridian, at 0 degrees longitude, was set through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, by an international conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884.
story:
Victor had until dinner, forty minutes, to figure out how to name the exact spot of any city on Earth, because tomorrow morning Mr. Dang was holding the geography club's map challenge and only two kids could enter. Riaan and Nathanael were already at his kitchen table, one holding an atlas, the other a chocolate-chip bag.

"Okay," Victor said, spreading out the world map. "Every city gets two numbers. Up and down, and side to side." He traced a finger down from the North Pole. "Mr. Dang called this one the prime meridian. Zero degrees longitude." He stopped where the line crossed London, at a little town called Greenwich.

"Wait," said Nathanael, spraying crumbs. "Why is the zero there? Why not in Cairo or somewhere?"

Victor leaned back in his chair, and suddenly he was somewhere else entirely. Last summer, in London with his parents, he had stood in a courtyard at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich with one foot on a metal strip set into the pavement. A tour guide beside him had told her group that the line ran straight through the observatory, and that an international conference had picked it, way back in 1884. Victor had asked where the conference happened, expecting London, and she had laughed and said Washington, D.C., all the way across the ocean. He had thought that was the strangest thing: the world's zero chosen in America, planted in England.

He snapped back to the kitchen. "Because of a vote," he said. "There was a big international conference in Washington, D.C., in 1884, and they decided the zero line of longitude would run through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. That's why it's the prime meridian." Riaan wrote it in his notebook under FACTS THAT SOUND FAKE.

"Okay but the challenge," said Riaan, checking the clock. "Twenty-five minutes."

They drilled each other. Victor learned to classify cities by hemisphere: positive longitude east, negative west, and latitude climbing toward ninety at the poles. Nathanael kept mixing up the two numbers until Victor said, "Think of it like a rodent in a tube. It runs along the equator first, then climbs a ladder. Side to side, then up and down." Nathanael narrowed his eyes, then nodded slowly. "Fine. Rodents. Got it."

When Victor's mom called that dinner was in five minutes, they tried the hardest practice question. Victor read out the numbers, ran his finger along the map, and tapped a small dot in South America. "Lima! That's Lima, Peru!"

Nathanael checked the answer key, jumped up, and knocked over the chocolate chips.

"That," Victor shouted, "is obsolete chocolate now. Tomorrow we win."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A bylaw is a rule made by a local government, such as a city or town council, and it applies only within that municipality.
story:
Maria pressed her petition against the wooden railing outside courtroom three and counted the signatures for the fourth time. Thirty-one. The skateboard ban at Hartley Park had ruined the whole summer for her and half the kids at the community centre, and the big court date was today. She had assumed, when she started collecting names, that some faraway national law was behind the ban, something written in the capital that judges enforced like weather. Her mother had driven her downtown, the bus having been too slow, and now the hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper.

Raelynn arrived first, out of breath, then Coralie, who carried the poster they had made with a photograph of the park's empty diagonal path cutting across the grass. "Did you bring the signatures?" Coralie whispered. Mr. Bélanger, the crossing guard from their street, was waiting on the bench by the water fountain. He nodded at Maria's folder. "Good," he said. "Now, whose office are you taking those to?"

Maria stopped halfway down the corridor. "The judge's," she said slowly. "Isn't he deciding about the ban today?" Mr. Bélanger's eyebrows lifted, but he only pointed at the directory board on the wall. Maria read it, and read it again. The hearing behind door three was about a parking dispute, nothing to do with skateboards. Nothing here was about skateboards at all. Her stomach tightened as the pieces shifted. If the ban wasn't on the docket, then nobody upstairs had created it. Then who?

She ran the facts like a test in her head. The sign at the park said "By Order of the Town." A bylaw, she remembered the word now from the community centre flyer, is a rule made by a local government, such as a city or town council, and it applies only within that municipality. That was the hidden pattern. The capital had never heard of Hartley Park. The town council had voted on this, which meant the town council could undo it, and a judge was the wrong door entirely.

Maria turned away from the courtroom and marched toward the front doors, the others hurrying behind her. "We're in the wrong building," she said. "We need town hall, and we need a councillor." At the entrance she stopped, took a breath, and squared her pages against her chest. The number thirty-one had not changed, but its meaning had. "Coralie, which bus transports us closest to the council offices?" Coralie was already pointing at the route map bolted beside the glass. "That one. Leaves in four minutes." They ran.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Victoria's problem was the classroom plant, the one by the window that had been dropping leaves since Tuesday while the identical plant by the door stayed green. Nobody had touched either one, or so everyone claimed, and Mr. Mensah had written on the board, "What do you think is happening? Test it." That was the assignment, due Friday.

"I think someone's knocking it when they walk past," Lina said, poking the sick plant's pot. "That side gets hallway traffic."

"Then the leaves on the traffic side should be the ones falling," Victoria said, crouching to look. She counted. Seven leaves on the floor, but five had come from the window side, which nobody could bump without climbing over a desk. Her guess about bumping was dead, and she hadn't even done anything yet.

Leah wandered over with her notebook. "You could say people are bumping it, that's a theory."

"Mr. Mensah would fail you for that," Victoria said. "A theory is an explanation that's been tested over and over, like evolution. What I have is a hypothesis, an idea still being tested." She said it fast, because her older brother had gotten this wrong at dinner on Sunday and their mother had made them look it up before anyone got dessert.

So she tested. Her second hypothesis was cold air leaking through the window frame, and she taped a strip of paper along the edge and watched it. The paper didn't flutter. Hypothesis two, dead. Lina's guess, dead. Leah suggested Victoria summarize the results in a chart, which Victoria did, feeling less like a scientist and more like an accountant of failures.

On Friday morning she came in early and found Mr. Mensah watering the door plant from a blue pitcher. When he moved to the window plant, he skipped it. "That one gets watered Mondays and Thursdays," he said. "The blue pitcher is plain water. The green pitcher, that one's fertilizer, and the window plant hates it."

Victoria wrote her final line: the hidden cause was the watering can. Mr. Mensah read it, and read her two dead hypotheses below it, and drew a small check mark beside each crossed-out idea.

"Most people hide the wrong ones," he said.

"Mine were very wrong," Victoria said. "They deserved to be seen."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Ryder logged into the castle siege lobby and found his whole squad already there, arguing in the chat window. Luc had typed "Okay." in reply to Aimee's plan, and Aimee had fired back with "wow, someone woke up angry." Ryder read the message twice. He had seen Luc type "okay" a hundred times and nobody got upset, so what made this one different? The only thing he could spot was the tiny dot at the end.

He typed his own experiment into the private message box, where only Luc could see it. First he sent "fine" and waited. Luc replied with a thumbs-up. Then Ryder sent "fine." and watched Luc's answer stall. "why are you mad at me," Luc typed. Ryder grinned so wide his mom, passing behind the couch with laundry, gave him a suspicious look.

"come to team voice," Ryder said, and Luc clicked in. "I'm not mad," Luc insisted, sounding genuinely baffled. "I just put a period because it looked tidy." Ryder told him about the thing he'd read on Ms. Watanabe's classroom poster last week, that a small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one. Luc digested this in silence for a moment. "So my tidy punctuation makes me sound like a villain," he said. "That's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard. And also completely true, isn't it."

Back in the public lobby chat, where anyone could read, Aimee was still stewing. Ryder knew the lobby was a public space while their private messages were their own, so he typed carefully in the open window: "luc did a science experiment on you." Then, privately, he coached Luc through an apology: "ok!!" with two exclamation marks and no period anywhere. Luc hovered over the send button like a knight deciding whether a charge was voluntary or doomed. "This feels illegal," he muttered into the headset. He sent it anyway.

Aimee's reply appeared in the lobby chat a second later: "ok!! :)" The siege horn blared, the gates rattled, and all three of them stopped typing at once, because the battering ram was already halfway up the hill and none of them had picked a position. "Towers, towers!" Ryder shouted, and Luc, punctuation finally forgotten, sprinted for the stairs.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A persuasive essay is stronger when it states the best opposing argument fairly and then answers it; this answer is called a rebuttal.
story:
Grayson stared at the blank page in his notebook like it had insulted his family. Five paragraphs, an introduction, a conclusion, and the whole thing had to actually convince someone of something. He had chosen his topic, "Why the school day should start an hour later," and then written exactly nothing for eleven minutes.

"You look like your brain is rebelling," said Rio, dropping into the chair across from him in the library. Rio was writing about cafeteria pizza and had somehow already filled a page.

"It is. I have the introduction, sort of, and three reasons. But it feels like I'm just yelling at nobody." Grayson turned his notebook around. "Sleep helps memory, bus routes would be safer in daylight, and, uh, teenagers."

Brielle slid her own essay over. Her topic was no phones in class, and she had written a whole paragraph that started with "Some people say phones help students look things up." Then she answered it, explaining that kids with phones also checked them every few minutes, which broke focus.

"Wait, why are you being nice to the other side?" Grayson asked. "Isn't that helping them win?"

"It's called a rebuttal," Brielle said. "You state their best argument fairly and then answer it."

Mr. Reyes, passing by with a cart of returned biographies, paused. "Hers is the one I'd keep reading," he said, and rolled on before Grayson could interrogate him.

Grayson chewed his pencil. That was the pattern, then. It wasn't enough to stack up reasons like bricks; the strong move was to walk over to the other side, pick up their best weapon, and hand it back broken. But he had to test it, because it sounded completely backward. He flipped to a clean page and wrote the opposing argument as fairly as he could: starting school later means ending later, so sports practice and after-school jobs get squeezed, and in winter, students would walk home in the dark.

Rio read over his shoulder. "Okay, that's actually a decent point against you."

"I know. That's why it goes in." Grayson then wrote his answer: the schedule could shift only forty minutes, and study hall could move to the end of the day, so practice would lose almost nothing. It felt strange, like admitting a weakness made him stronger instead of weaker.

"Here's my critique," Rio said, holding up a finger. "Your introduction says 'In this essay I will' like a robot wrote it."

"An impulsive part of me wants to throw this notebook in the return bin," Grayson said, "but fine." He rewrote the opening with a hook about falling asleep in first period, and it actually sounded like a human being.

The next day, Mr. Reyes handed the essays back. At the top of Grayson's page was a circled A minus and one comment: "The rebuttal does the heavy lifting. Nice work." Grayson read it three times, then slid it across the table to Brielle.

"Told you," she said.

"You told me," Grayson said. "Rio, we're adding rebuttals to yours too. Even the pizza essay."

"Especially the pizza essay," Rio said. "Some people say pizza is unhealthy, and I intend to destroy them."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying two denominators together always gives a common denominator, though it is not always the smallest one.
story:
Florence had failed the fractions quiz on Tuesday, and on Wednesday Mr. Ricci handed her a hall pass to the library with the words "practice pages, back table" written on it. She sat down with her pencil, her eraser, and the worst problem she had ever seen: one third plus one fourth.

She could picture one third of a pizza. She could picture one fourth of a pizza. But she could not picture adding them, because the slices were different sizes, and nobody had drawn anything on the page. There was a hidden rule somewhere, and she meant to conquer it before Friday's retake.

A folded note slid across the table. Caroline grinned and pointed at the ceiling as if she had nothing to do with it. Inside, in quick handwriting, it said: "Just times the bottom numbers. 3 x 4 = 12. Fix the tops to match. It works for minus too. Signed, a friend."

Florence tested it on a scrap paper. One third became four twelfths, one fourth became three twelfths, and seven twelfths came out clean. She tried two fifths minus one third: bottoms gave fifteen, the tops became six and five, and the answer was one fifteenth. Then she tried one half plus one fourth. The note's trick turned them into four eighths and two eighths, which made six eighths, and she had to simplify all the way back down to three fourths. It worked every time, but the answers came out fatter than they needed to be. It was ironic that the fastest method left her with the longest simplifying.

She slid her own note back across the table. "Who wrote this? Because six eighths means extra reducing. Why not just use eighths... I mean fourths... for half and fourth?"

Caroline held up both hands. Then Irene, two seats over, lowered her magazine. "That was me," she admitted. "I found it in my sister's notebook. Six eighths is still right. Mr. Ricci just makes you simplify at the end."

Florence looked at her scrap paper, where the common denominator had steered each problem like a rudder, keeping both fractions headed the same way no matter how big the numbers got. She wrote a new note in careful letters and passed it down the row: "Retake Friday. Meet me here Thursday. Bring your sister's notebook and I'll bring my simplifying."

Irene read it, nodded, and gave her a thumbs up.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediation usually ends with both sides agreeing on specific actions they will each take, so each person knows exactly what they promised.
story:
At dinner on Friday, Taylor pushed her noodles around her plate while her dad asked about her day. "Janessa and Elena aren't speaking to each other," she said. "They both got mad about the group poster, and each one wants me on her side." Her mom set down the water pitcher and said that sounded like a hard spot. Taylor nodded, but she was already thinking about lunch on Monday, when she would have to sit somewhere.

On Saturday, Taylor tried to fix it. She called Janessa first, then Elena, and finally got them together on the back steps of her building. "Can't you two just be friends again?" she asked. They both shrugged and said fine, and Taylor felt exceptional, like a peacemaker in a movie. For about one afternoon. By Sunday night, Janessa had texted that Elena was "acting like nothing happened," and Elena had texted that Janessa still hadn't sent her half of the poster notes. The friendship had snapped right back into silence, and Taylor couldn't see why. They had said yes. That was supposed to be the ending.

At Sunday dinner, her grandmother asked what was wrong, and Taylor explained the whole thing. "They agreed," she said, "and then it fell apart anyway." She kept turning it over while the dishes were being cleared. Then a thought slid into place, quiet and surprising. Janessa and Elena had agreed to a feeling, not to anything they could actually do. Taylor remembered the student council thing Ms. Popal had run last spring, where two boys who'd clashed over gym equipment had shaken hands at the end. But Ms. Popal hadn't stopped at the handshake. She'd made each boy say exactly what he would do the next morning, one getting the balls first on odd days, the other on even. Taylor hadn't understood that part at the time. She'd thought it was just fuss. Now she suspected it was the actual trick.

Monday at lunch, she tried to modify her plan. She sat between Janessa and Elena at the corner table and said, "Saying you're friends again doesn't tell you anything. You have to each promise a thing. A real thing you'll do." Elena frowned. "Like what?" "Like, Janessa sends you the poster notes by tonight, and you stop saying she ruined the layout in front of everybody." Janessa's mouth opened to argue, then closed. "Fine," she said. "If she actually stops saying that." Elena crossed her arms, thinking, while the cafeteria clattered around them. "Fine," she said at last. "Tonight. But if the notes aren't there by eight, this whole deal is off."

Taylor watched them eat in careful silence, and she couldn't tell yet whether it would hold. Maybe by Tuesday they'd be laughing, and maybe they'd be worse than before, and she honestly didn't know which. She only knew that now each of them had a promise with edges on it, something she could point to if it broke. She picked up her tray and heard Janessa mutter, "By eight, remember."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
The locker room smelled like rubber mats and deodorant, and Matthew was holding his phone up to his own throat like a tiny scientist. "Watch," he said. "I'm going to hum, and you're going to see if anything moves."

Gregoire, still lacing his shoes, looked skeptical. "Nothing's going to move. It's inside your neck."

"That's the whole point. It's hidden." Matthew hummed a low note, then a high one, then the high one again, and this time his voice cracked right down the middle, like a floorboard giving way. Both of them froze.

"Did you hear that?" Matthew grabbed Gregoire's shoulder. "That's the fourth time this week. Monday in choir, twice on Wednesday, and now here. It's a pattern. Something is causing it, and I want to know what."

Summer came around the corner of the lockers with her bag over one shoulder. "You two are weird. It's just a voice crack. Everyone's brother does it."

"No, it's not just anything." Matthew paced between the benches, thinking out loud. "In choir yesterday, Benjie cracked on the high note in the second verse. Ms. Adeyemi didn't even stop the piano. She just said, 'His larynx is growing, that's all. The vocal folds inside it are getting longer and thicker.' Then she kept playing."

Gregoire frowned. "The what?"

"The larynx. It's in your throat, and the vocal folds are inside it. When they get longer and thicker, that's why the voice gets deeper. And while it's happening, the voice cracks." He pointed at his own neck. "That's the hidden cause. You can't see it, but I can test it."

Summer crossed her arms. "Test it how?"

Matthew pulled up a voice memo app on his phone. "The narrator of this app reads the time out loud. Listen." He tapped record, hummed his low note, then the high one, and crack. It split again, right on schedule. He played it back, and the three of them leaned in to hear the wobble in the middle of the sound.

"That recording is proof," Matthew said. "Does the crack signify the folds are growing right now, or does it mean they've already grown? Maybe every crack means I'm one crack closer to a deep voice."

Summer tilted her head, thinking. "Actually, that makes sense. My brother's voice used to do that all the time. I thought it was random. Now I think it was a rule the whole time."

"Exactly!" Matthew said. "I used to think cracks were embarrassing, like tripping in front of everyone. But now I think they're more like..." He searched for the word. "Like construction signs. Voice under construction."

Gregoire laughed and stood up. "Okay, I changed my mind. This is actually kind of great. So when's it going to be done?"

"No idea," Matthew said, stuffing his phone in his pocket and slinging his bag over his shoulder. "But next rehearsal, when we hit the high note in the second verse, I'm going for it."

He jogged for the door, humming all the way down the hall.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The independent variable is the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens.
story:
Jonathan knelt in the dirt between the strawberry beds, holding a pale leaf up to the light. Two weeks ago Ms. Harper's plants had been thick and green; now half of them drooped, and the pale ones had a dusty look he couldn't name. He wanted to know why, because if it spread to his own bed, his whole crop would be gone.

He remembered last summer, when the wilting in his grandmother's garden had seemed contagious, jumping from tomato to tomato until nothing was left. He had been eight then, and he had just watched. This time he would do something.

His first idea was that the pale plants were getting too much sun, or maybe the wrong amount of water. So he moved two sick plants into the shade of the bean trellis and, at the same time, gave them extra water every morning. Within a week both had turned a healthier green. "See?" he told Katelynn, who had come over to pinch off strawberry hulls for the fruit salad her mother was making. "It worked."

Katelynn frowned at the two recovered plants. "Worked how? You changed two things at once. Shade and water. Which one fixed them?" Jonathan opened his mouth and then closed it. He tried to distinguish the two effects in his memory, but the plants had improved together, and he couldn't untangle them. "I can't tell," he admitted. "I ruined my own test."

"No, you learned something," Katelynn said, dropping a hull into the bucket. "Ms. Harper calls it the independent variable. It's the one thing you change on purpose to see what happens." She said it the way she recited lines for the spring play, quick and certain.

So Jonathan started over. He put one sick plant in shade with normal water, and gave another full sun with extra water. He watered a third exactly as before, in full sun, as a comparison. He labeled each pot with a popsicle stick and wrote the plan in his notebook, his pencil scratching against the page while a bee droned somewhere behind the snap peas.

Eight days later the shaded plant stood green and firm, the extra-water plant still drooped, and the untouched one had gone almost white. He ran his thumb along the healthy leaf and heard Katelynn laughing by the fence. "So it was the sun after all," she called. "Told you the water was a red herring." Jonathan cupped the small plant in his hands and carried it toward the cool shadow of the trellis.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Closing a switch completes the circuit so current flows; opening it makes a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once.
story:
Nathan had promised Ms. Jean-Louis that his model house would be ready for the science fair, and the fair was tomorrow. He spread the parts on the picnic table in his backyard: a battery, a folded metal switch, a small bulb, and three wires with clips on the ends. Louis-Philippe sat across from him, and Nikki had left a note taped to the toolbox before her soccer game. It read, "My little brother wants a house where the lights really work. Don't give up. Bring me a photo when it lights." Nathan read it twice, then clipped a wire to each end of the battery, touched the free ends to the bulb, and grinned when it glowed. The hard part was the switch.

He unclipped one wire, clipped it to the switch instead, and added a third wire from the switch back around to the bulb. When he squeezed the switch shut, nothing happened. He squeezed it again, harder, and still nothing. "Maybe the battery's dead," Louis-Philippe said, holding it up to the sun, where the light refracted through the old glass jar of lemonade beside it and threw a bright stripe across the table. "No, it just lit a second ago," Nathan said. He borrowed the lemonade jar's lid and scraped the crusty clip with its edge, because leaked battery gunk could be corrosive, and the wire needed clean metal to bite onto. Still nothing.

Nathan sat back and thought. The bulb had worked before the switch went in. So the trouble had to be somewhere between the switch and the bulb. He lifted each wire and tugged gently, one at a time, and the third wire came loose in his hand, its clip barely hanging on. He pressed it tight onto the bulb contact and squeezed the switch. The bulb lit. He let go, and it went dark. He squeezed again, and it came back.

"We should show it with two bulbs," Louis-Philippe said, adding a second one into the loop. Nathan closed the switch and both bulbs glowed. Then he opened it, and both cut out in the same instant, no flicker, no one bulb lingering. "That's the whole trick," Nathan said. "Closing the switch completes the loop, so the current flows. Open it and there's a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once." He took a photo of the glowing little house and sent it to Nikki. Her reply buzzed back within a minute: a thumbs-up and the words, "Tell my brother's category at the fair to watch out." Nathan clipped the switch closed one more time, just to watch the windows light up.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: A receipt lists every item and the amount paid, so reading it before leaving the till catches a scanning mistake while it is easy to fix.
story:
Emmett stood at the kitchen counter holding a five-dollar bill and a note that read "2% milk, one jug." His mom had added a second line in smaller writing: "Also bread if under three dollars." He considered this an amendment to the original mission, and missions with amendments felt official.

"Take your phone," his mom said.

"I don't need a phone to buy milk."

"That's not what the phone is for. It's so I can call you."

"So the phone is for you," Emmett said, and pocketed it anyway, because arguing with a radical idea like that was pointless. He had walked to school a hundred times, but the corner store was different territory. Nobody had ever made him count change before. At school, Karlee had once dared Arman to eat a crayon for two dollars, and Arman had counted that change twice, so Emmett knew it mattered.

The store smelled like floor cleaner and oranges. He found the milk, found the bread, which was two dollars and eighty-nine cents, and carried both to the till. The cashier scanned everything while looking past Emmett at the parking lot. Then she held out a small paper slip along with his change. Emmett counted the coins in his palm first, then, because the receipt was there and his hands were free, he read it.

The milk was on it twice. Two jugs of milk, listed one after the other, same price, same everything, and he only had one jug. He had one jug and one loaf of bread, and the receipt said he had paid for two jugs and one loaf.

"Um," Emmett said. "It says milk twice, but I only bought one."

The cashier stopped looking at the parking lot. She squinted at the screen, tapped something, and handed him back a toonie. "Good catch, buddy."

He read the receipt one more time right there at the till, before he stepped away, because the mistake had been easy to fix in the store and he suspected it would be harder to fix from his kitchen. Now it said one milk, one bread, and the numbers matched his change.

At home he set the milk on the counter, the bread beside it, and the coins in a neat row, and slid the receipt across to his mom. "They scanned the milk twice," he said. "The receipt says everything you bought. You just have to read it before you leave."

His mom held it up to the light, as if checking for a watermark. "From now on," she said, "you're in charge of receipts."

"I accept," Emmett said, "no amendments."

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: The slope of a line is its rise over its run: how many units it goes up or down for each unit it moves to the right.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen table smelled like sawdust and maple syrup, and Taylor had spread her graph paper across it before he'd even finished the dishes. Neve sat across from her, turning a pencil end over end.

"It has to actually work," Neve said. She wanted to build the skateboard ramp this weekend, and she wanted it to be the best one on the block. "Not just look cool on paper."

"That's the part I keep messing up." Taylor frowned at her drawing. Two of her lines crossed the grid in different places, and she didn't know which one was right. The math homework said to solve for y, then plot the line, but the numbers kept sliding around in her head. She looked at the window, where the luminous afternoon light made the grid's blue lines shimmer, and then back down.

"Wait," she said. "Forget the numbers for a second. Just count squares." She put her pencil tip on the first point and traced along her line. "One unit to the right, and two units up. One right, two up again. Same every time."

"Like stairs," Neve said, leaning over. "Same size stairs all the way."

"Ms. Watanabe called that the slope," Taylor said. "The rise over the run. How many units it goes up for each unit it moves to the right." She checked her second line the same way. One right, two up. Both lines climbed exactly alike, so they had to be the same line, just drawn from different starting points.

"So the ramp goes up two for every one across," Neve said. "Steep."

"Too steep, maybe. We can exclude that one and try one that rises less." Taylor drew a gentler line, one up for every one across, and labeled it.

Neve grabbed the graph paper and held it up to the window. "This one. I'm measuring the boards tonight."

"Bring the leftovers," Taylor said. "Grandpa made pancakes."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder.
story:
Harrison stood at the bus stop with the plastic bag looped over one wrist, a carton of whole milk inside and eighty-five cents of change pressed flat in his palm. He counted it again, because that was part of the errand, the part his dad had drilled: hand over the five, get the right coins back. Two quarters, three dimes, a nickel. Right. The afternoon bus sighed past without stopping, and Noemie leaned on the pole beside him, unwrapping a granola bar.

"You look like you're solving something," she said.

"Milk's gone sour twice this week," Harrison said. "Both cartons, before the date on the side. That's not normal." He turned the problem over the way he sorted books at the library, deciding what genre a thing belonged to. This one was a mystery, and mysteries had clues.

"But we bought it fresh," Noemie said. "So it's not the store."

"Or the store," Harrison said slowly, "or the trip home, or the fridge. The milk sits in all three places." The synthetic seat of the bus shelter was warm under his legs, and he watched the traffic pass while he assessed it. The store sold a lot of milk; nobody else was complaining. The walk home took eight minutes in a cold bag. The fridge, though, the fridge he had never once checked.

When the next bus came they got on, and at his stop Harrison carried the carton straight to the kitchen. There was a little thermometer sitting on the middle shelf, a thing his mother used for nothing he had ever noticed. He read it: six degrees Celsius. He dug the fridge manual out of the junk drawer, and there on page three was the advice, printed plain: food safety agencies said to keep a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder. Six was warmer than four. The dial inside had been nudged, probably when someone had crammed the Thanksgiving leftovers in a month ago and shoved the shelf around.

He turned the dial one click colder and waited, watching the thermometer like it owed him money. By the time he had eaten his snack the little line had crept down past four. He wrote 4°C on a sticky note and pressed it beside the dial, so nobody would move it again without knowing.

The next morning the milk tasted cold and sweet. Harrison poured it over his cereal and thought about the new carton waiting in the fridge, the one he had bought and counted change for all by himself. He put the sticky note edge straight, then took a long drink from the glass.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: In his Rhetoric, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence.
story:
Aaron tapped his pencil against the library table until the eraser bounced. Mr. Brennan wanted a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction and a conclusion, and Aaron had decided to argue for a longer recess. The trouble was that his first paragraph sounded like a list of demands, and nobody ever gave in to demands.

A grandfather who shelved books on Tuesdays paused beside him, breathing the smell of old paper. He squinted at Aaron's notes. "Ethos, pathos, logos," he read. "Aristotle described three ways to persuade in his Rhetoric." He slid a book across the table, tapped the cover, and moved on to his cart.

Aaron opened the book. Ethos was the speaker's credibility, which meant people had to trust you. Pathos was the audience's emotions. Logos was logic and evidence. He copied the three words onto his napkin and, on the walk home, worked out a test. In the cafeteria the next day he tried each one separately. "I read a whole study about recess," he told Carina, laying out numbers, how scores fluctuate week to week but climb for classes with more playtime, and how kids who get the flu vaccine miss fewer days. Carina nodded along. But Megane just poked at her noodles until Aaron said, "Remember how the little kids stood at the fence in the rain yesterday, watching the minutes run out?" Her shoulders dropped, and she signed his petition on the spot.

So Aaron built all three into his essay. His introduction mentioned that he had counted recess minutes for two weeks, since a guy with data was a guy worth believing. The body paragraphs stacked the study, the flu comparison, and the image of kids at the fence. His conclusion asked Mr. Brennan directly for a reply, because a request had to be explicit, not buried in the middle.

On Friday, Mr. Brennan read it during silent work, then looked up. "Twelve extra minutes," he said, holding the page. "You argue like a Greek. Aaron, this goes on the wall outside the office, where the principal walks past twice a day."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground, like granite, has large crystals, while rock that cools fast at the surface, like basalt, has tiny ones.
story:
The creek ran shallow and loud behind the tents, and David crouched at its edge with three rocks lined up on a flat stone. Mr. Haile had promised that anyone who could sort a handful of rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic before the campfire ended would win the last bag of peach candy. Trace had already filled his pockets and claimed two sparkly chunks, which David was beginning to resent, since Trace mostly wanted the candy and not the rocks.

"Those two are the same kind," Trace said, holding out his finds. "Both speckly. Both pretty."

David turned them over. One was pale and glittering, salt-and-pepper, every fleck big enough to see. The other was dark and plain, fine as flour, with no sparkle at all. He wet a finger and rubbed the dark one clean, but it stayed dull. That night, by flashlight, he wrote a note on the back of the trail map and slid it across the log to Ariyah, who was sorting pebbles beside him.

"Both of these cooled from melted rock," the note said. "Igneous. But look close. The speckly one has big crystals. The dark one has tiny ones. Meet me at the creek at breakfast."

In the morning Ariyah was already there, turning the two rocks in the light. "My gran has a granite countertop," she said slowly. "It looks just like the speckly one. She says the granite cooled slowly, way underground, so the crystals got big." She set it down and picked up the dark pebble. "This one cooled fast at the surface. I think it's basalt."

"So the crystal size is like a clock," David said. "Big means slow, underground. Tiny means fast, up top where it cools quick." He lined them up: the granite, the basalt, then a layered brown rock with stripes like fudge, which had to be sedimentary, pressed out of mud and sand. Trace came down the path with his pockets still full, saw the arrangement, and changed his mind about the whole game. He dumped his rocks beside theirs and started hunting for something striped, because now he wanted to find the third kind, not just the candy.

By the fire that evening, Mr. Haile walked the line of sorted stones with his hands behind his back. He stopped at the granite and the basalt sitting side by side, and asked nothing at all, only nodded. Then he handed the peach candy to all three of them at once. David bit into his, and the sweet nectar of it ran down his chin while Ariyah held the basalt up to the last orange light, close enough to see the tiny crystals glint.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Paraphrasing, or restating what someone said in your own words, shows them they were heard and lets them correct any misunderstanding.
story:
The rain hammering the classroom windows was supposed to be the most interesting thing about Tuesday, until Maryam slammed her tray down at the table next to Ryder and refused to look at him. Alice set her sandwich aside. Yesterday the three of them had been planning the science fair project together, a volcano with molten lava made from baking soda and vinegar, and today Maryam and Ryder were acting like strangers.

"He said my poster was ugly," Maryam hissed, stabbing her fork into the pasta.

"I never said that," Ryder shot back, his ears going red. "I said the layout was confusing."

Alice's first idea was to pick whoever seemed most upset, but she stopped herself. Ms. Sánchez had put a poster on the wall last week about solving conflicts, and one line kept floating back to Alice: paraphrasing, it said, meant restating what someone said in your own words. She hadn't really understood it then. Now, watching her two friends talk past each other, she decided to try it as an experiment, the way she'd test anything else.

"So, Maryam," Alice said slowly, "you heard him say the poster itself was ugly, like the whole thing, not just the layout." Maryam nodded, arms still crossed, but her shoulders came down an inch. "And Ryder, you meant only that the parts were hard to follow, not that it looked bad." Ryder nodded too. Alice kept going, restating each of their words back to them, and something strange happened. Maryam frowned and said, "Wait. That's not exactly what I meant. I was mostly embarrassed because I stayed up until eleven making it." Ryder blinked. "I didn't know that. I thought you slapped it together at lunch."

That was the crack in the whole fight. Nobody had actually said the poster was ugly; the hurt had grown out of a sentence that was never spoken, the way the garden's dead leaves would decompose into something that looked completely different from what they'd been. Alice felt her own ears go warm. It wasn't a full fix, but Maryam had turned slightly toward Ryder instead of toward the window, where the precipitation still streaked the glass in long silver lines.

"Could I try the layout again," Maryam said, "if you help with the labels?"

"Yeah," Ryder said. "And you can pick the lava color." He grinned. "As long as it's still molten orange."

Alice picked up her sandwich again, and outside the rain finally began to soften.

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, showing that atoms contain small, negatively charged particles.
story:
Lucy counted her styrofoam balls for the third time. Twelve orange, twelve gray, and a bag of tiny blue beads rolling around the bottom of the box like they wanted to escape. In forty minutes the judges would walk the gymnasium floor, and her model of an atom still looked like a lumpy planet with random beads taped wherever they fit.

"What did you do, throw them on there?" asked Lyric, who was setting up the volcano two tables over. Lyric's baking soda smelled like actual science. Lucy's table smelled like glue.

"The protons and neutrons go in the middle," Lucy said, stabbing a gray ball with a toothpick. "It's the electrons I can't figure out. Ms. Sow said they aren't just stuck in one spot."

Everley wandered over, still holding her half-finished poster about magnets. "I read about that at the library yesterday. In 1897, J. J. Thomson discovered the electron. Before him, nobody knew atoms had small pieces like that at all."

"Wait," Lucy said. "So out of the three particles, the electron was found first?"

"First and only, for a while," Everley said.

Lucy stared at her lumpy planet. If the electron was discovered before the protons and neutrons were, then it wasn't just decoration around the edge. It mattered. She pictured the bead paths looping outward from the center, like rings, each electron in its own lane instead of wherever the tape happened to land. She grabbed the beads and started threading them onto loops of wire.

The glue was still tacky when Ms. Sow stopped at her table, but the electron rings spun on their wires, one bead per lane, the whole thing turning slowly under the gym lights.

"A hidden cause, an unseen pattern, and a working model," Ms. Sow said. "That's a revolution in thinking, Lucy."

Lucy gave the smallest ring a push and watched the blue bead ride its orbit around and around.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
story:
Charlie sat cross-legged on her bed with a box of tissues and her stuffed kangaroo, Pip, wedged under one arm like a joey riding in a pouch. She had been staring at the same page of her book for ten minutes, which was how she knew the flu was winning. Her head thumped, her throat felt like sandpaper, and her mom had diagnosed her that morning with one look and a thermometer: 102.3, back to bed, no arguments.

She reached for her phone and called Sam. "When did you start feeling sick?" she asked, trying to sound assertive instead of whiny, because whiny made people hang up.

"Tuesday night," Sam said. "The headache came first, then the fever. Jude got it too. Remember, we were all at the sleepover Saturday."

Charlie flopped back against her pillows. Saturday. They had built a blanket fort in Jude's basement and stayed up until two, sharing popcorn from the same bowl, three girls with their heads together over one flashlight. Nobody had coughed. Nobody had seemed the least bit sick. That was the part that kept snagging in her mind like a splinter in a sock.

"How could we all catch it from each other if nobody was sick yet?" she asked.

Sam was quiet for a second. "My mom said people with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms. So somebody at the sleepover already had it Saturday. We just couldn't tell."

"One day before," Charlie repeated. Jude had seemed fine, but so had she, and so had Sam. It could have been any of them, passing it around in the blanket fort, invisible as a draft. She thought about how she'd pressed close between them for the scary story, giggling, and how she'd do it again even knowing what she knew now. Maybe. She wasn't sure yet.

"Mom's bringing soup," Sam said. "Call you tomorrow?"

"Deal." Charlie set down the phone, pulled the blanket up to her chin, and hugged Pip tighter against her aching ribs.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet.
story:
The kitten's name was Biscuit, and she rode home from the shelter in a cardboard box with air holes, meowing like a tiny angry trumpet. Jordan's whole family was vegetarian, so his mom had already bought a bag of plant-based cat food, and Biscuit sniffed it, looked at Jordan as if he had personally insulted her, and walked away.

That had been three days ago, and Biscuit had barely eaten since. Her coat, glossy on day one, was starting to look dull. "She's going to deteriorate if this keeps up," Rosalynn said, crouching on the sidewalk in front of Jordan's house while Biscuit stalked a leaf. "My grandpa uses that word about his fence. It means falling apart bit by bit."

Jordan thought about the shelter volunteer who had squatted next to him, before the box, before any of this, and said, "Feed her what cats need, not what you eat." At the time he'd nodded without really listening. Now he stared at Biscuit, who had gone aggressive on a stick, batting it across the driveway like it owed her money, and an idea ticked in his head. Maybe the problem wasn't the food dish. Maybe it was what was in it. Cats, unlike his family, might actually need the stuff that comes from animal flesh. He remembered the volunteer's exact phrase and said it out loud, almost like a test: "Obligate carnivores. That's what she called cats."

"Sounds like a superhero team," Raelynn said from the porch, where she was holding an ice pack to her head after falling off the curb. "I might have a concussion, by the way."

"You fell eight inches."

"Concussions are serious."

Jordan marched inside and came back out with a can of actual meat cat food he'd found buried in the pantry. He set it down. Biscuit froze, whiskers forward, then charged across the driveway and shoved her whole face into the bowl.

"Told you," Jordan said, and scratched her ears while she ate like the leaf, the stick, and the vegetarian kibble had all been warm-ups for this moment.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
story:
On the third night of their trip to Taipei, Jeremy sat on the hotel bed with his notebook, trying to build five sentences in Mandarin about his family before bed. Ms. Ito had assigned it before the trip, and tomorrow the class would video-call from the hotel lobby at nine in the morning, Taipei time. He had his mother's phrasebook app, but no signal on his phone, and his older sister Sophie was asleep in the other bed.

The words for mother and father were easy enough. Then he reached his little brother Sam, who was actually not so little: Sam was his twin, born ten minutes after him. The app listed two different words, gēge and dìdi, and Jeremy realized the book expected him to know which one meant what. He texted his friend Lea, who was on the trip with her own family two floors up. "Do you know if dìdi means older or younger brother?" Her reply came back fast: "No idea. My book just says gēge means older brother."

Jeremy sat with that for a moment. If gēge meant older brother, then dìdi had to be the other one, the younger. He tested the idea against the sentences he had already copied: Lea's phrasebook said "Wǒ yǒu yí gè gēge" for "I have an older brother." The pattern held. So for Sam, ten minutes younger, the word was dìdi. The realization felt like an insight landing softly: the language cared about something English never bothered to mark. Sophie stirred and muttered that his desk light was too bright, which did nothing except provoke him to angle the lamp away from her.

At the lobby call the next morning, Khadijah from Ms. Ito's class went first and described her two big brothers with gēge twice, smooth as anything. When Jeremy's turn came, he said, "Wǒ yǒu yí gè dìdi," and held up a photo of Sam on his ninth birthday. Ms. Ito smiled at the screen and asked, "Ten minutes younger?" Jeremy nodded. "Then dìdi is exactly right." Behind him, the hotel clerk, who had been listening, gave him a thumbs up and called out, "Hěn hǎo!" with infectious delight.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Many schools run peer mediation programs, in which trained students help classmates settle conflicts, usually with an adult supervisor available.
story:
At soccer practice on Thursday, Lianna and Bennett stopped speaking to each other, which was a problem because they were the two center midfielders and had to pass to each other. Rebecca found out why when she sat between them on the bench, catching water bottles. Lianna claimed Bennett had told the coach she was too slow for the starting lineup. Bennett swore he had only said the opposite, that Lianna deserved to start. Neither of them would budge.

Rebecca had finished peer mediation training at school only two weeks before. "You know I trained as a peer mediator," she said carefully. "Want me to try the steps on you two?" Mr. Kerr was watching the scrimmage from the far sideline, and she knew the rules said a trained student helps classmates settle conflicts with an adult supervisor available, so she checked with him first. He nodded and said he would stay where she could see him.

She sat Lianna and Bennett on the end of the bench, facing each other, and made herself a neutral spot in the middle, arms uncrossed, taking neither one's hand or side. "One at a time," she said. "Lianna, tell him what you heard, not what you think it meant."

Lianna took a breath. "Maya said you told the coach I was too slow."

Bennett's face went red. "I said you were the fastest player on the team. Maya must have heard the first half and missed the rest." He looked at the ground. "I was trying to get you more minutes, not fewer."

Rebecca noticed something she couldn't see directly, a hidden cause underneath the whole fight. Both of them had been scared of the same thing, losing their spot, and that fear had shaped what each of them believed. She tested the idea out loud. "So the fear of being benched is what this whole fight symbolizes, not anything either of you actually did?"

Lianna blinked. "I guess that's true. I was terrified about Saturday."

"Me too," Bennett admitted.

Rebecca asked what they needed from each other, which was the step she always forgot in practice role plays. Lianna asked him to come to her directly next time instead of talking to the coach behind her back. Bennett asked her not to believe Maya's version without checking. They agreed on both.

When Mr. Kerr called them back onto the field, Lianna stood up first and offered Bennett her fist. He bumped it. Then he passed her the ball, and she ran onto the grass with it, both of them chasing the play side by side.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many stores stock shelves 'first in, first out', putting older products at the front, so the carton with the latest date is often at the back.
story:
Thomas stood at the kitchen counter with ten dollars in his pocket and a note from his mother that said, simply, "Milk. Whole." It was his first solo mission to the corner store, three blocks away, and he had studied the route so many times that he could draw it with his eyes closed. He told his friend Raymond about it at breakfast, since Raymond had done the same run since he was ten.

"The hard part isn't the walking," Raymond said. "It's the change. The cashier talks fast and there's a line behind you, and you panic and shove everything in your pocket."

Thomas had a plan for that. He would count his money before he went in, then count the change at the counter, right there, in front of everyone, even if it took forever. He set out at four o'clock, when the sunlight refracted off the puddle at the end of his street in a way that made the whole puddle look like it was on fire. He walked past it carefully, as if it might be.

The store smelled like cardboard and oranges. He found the dairy case and picked up the first carton of whole milk. Then something stopped him. He looked at the date on top, then lifted the carton behind it. The date on that one was later. He checked a third carton, way at the back, and its date was later still. He stood there holding three cartons of milk like a man playing a very slow game of cards.

"That's first in, first out," said a woman reaching past him for cream. "Older stuff goes in front." She said it the way you'd mention the weather, then left with her cream.

Thomas slid his hand to the back and took the carton with the latest date. At the register he counted his change out loud, one coin at a time, while the man behind him sighed with what could only be described as despair. The cashier waited without complaint, which Thomas decided counted as a small act of kindness. He counted again on the way home, on the bench by the fire hydrant, and it was right: four dollars and sixty-one cents.

Back in the kitchen, his mother opened the bag, looked at the carton, and turned it over. "You got the one with the latest date," she said. "How?"

"The front ones were older," Thomas said. "The good ones hide at the back." He put the change on the counter, coin by coin, in a neat silver line, and slid the last quarter into place with one finger.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: The least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly; for quarters and sixths it is 12.
story:
Paige leaned over the glass counter at Mr. Tran's corner store, staring at a chocolate bar broken into pieces. Mr. Tran had cracked it into fourths on one side and sixths on the other, because a shipment had arrived crushed and he was selling the pieces by weight.

"Two dollars for the whole thing," he said, "but you three have to split it and split the price too, before the 4:15 bus comes. I close at four."

Paige, Marilyn, and Ryden had exactly sixteen minutes. Ryden wanted the fourths side because the pieces were bigger. Marilyn wanted the sixths side because there were more of them. Paige, who had gotten a D on last week's fraction quiz, just wanted everyone to pay a fair share.

"Okay," said Marilyn, pulling out a notebook on the counter. "One fourth plus one sixth. I'll use 24 as the denominator, because both numbers divide into it. That's six twenty-fourths plus four twenty-fourths, so ten twenty-fourths each if we each take some of both."

Ryden frowned at her numbers. "That works," he admitted, "but those are huge fractions. There has to be something smaller."

Paige had been making a quiet assumption all week, the one that had wrecked her quiz: that unlike denominators just couldn't be added, period. Now she stared at the broken bar itself. Sixths and fourths lay side by side, and she formulated a new idea out loud. "What if we chop every piece so they're all the same size? Like, cut each sixth in half and each fourth into three." She traced it with her finger on the chocolate. Fourths became twelfths. Sixths became twelfths.

"Twelve," Ryden said slowly. "Both 4 and 6 divide into it evenly."

"And it's smaller than 24," Marilyn said, surprise in her voice. She erased her work. "So the least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly. For quarters and sixths it's 12. I've been doing it the hard way all year." She laughed. "Ironic, right? More pieces, more math, same answer."

They counted: each of them would get three twelfths of the bar, which was a fourth, and pay fifty cents. Mr. Tran weighed the pieces, nodded, and rang it up as the bus rumbled toward the stop outside.

"Wrap it," Paige said, sliding her coins across the counter. "I have a quiz on Thursday, and this bar is coming with me."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: The bandwagon fallacy claims something must be right or good simply because many people believe it or do it.
story:
Emilie spread her draft across the library table and read her first paragraph out loud in a whisper. Her essay argued that the school should start a lacrosse team, and her strongest reason, the one she had put in the middle paragraph, was that everyone at school wanted it. She had asked around at lunch, and forty-two students had said yes. That felt like proof.

Drake sat down across from her, sliding a graphic novel aside. "Is that the lacrosse essay? Can I read it when you're done? My mom says I have to bring home something I wrote this week, and I want to see how a real one looks." He leaned over her paper.

"Sure," Emilie said. She pointed at her middle paragraph. "But something about this reason feels thin. Forty-two people want a team. So what?"

Drake read it and shrugged. "That's a lot of people."

Emilie tapped her pencil. Last week, she remembered, the whole cafeteria had lined up for the mystery meat special just because the line was long, and half of them had hated it. Everyone doing something had not made it good. She flipped to the glossary of her writing handbook and ran her finger down the F column. There it was: a named mistake where something is treated as right or good simply because many people believe it or do it.

"Oh," she said. "That's the bandwagon fallacy. My whole reason is a bandwagon fallacy."

"You can't build your essay on that?"

"Not and get a decent grade, I think." She crossed out the sentence and started testing a better reason: the school had no spring sport for kids who couldn't afford club fees, and a team would fix that. She wrote fast, hopeful now.

Ms. Kapoor passed their table and paused at the pile of crossed-out drafts. "Revising?"

"Testing," Emilie said, and slid the finished essay toward Drake.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The lights went out all over Grandma's street at exactly 7:14, because Chloe was watching the clock on the microwave when it died. She heard her grandmother sigh from the kitchen, then the scrape of a chair, then footsteps in the dark. "Well," Grandma said, "there go my plans to vacuum."

Chloe found the candles in the drawer by the stove, the drawer that held a flashlight with dead batteries, three rubber bands, and a letter she had never noticed before. It was addressed to Grandma in loopy handwriting, and while Grandma lit the candle, Chloe squinted at it by the flame. "Grandma, can I read this? It's from Haven's mom, from years ago." The wax seal had already been broken long ago, and the paper smelled like the inside of an old book.

Go ahead, Grandma said, so Chloe read it out loud, doing what she privately called her narrator voice, the one she used when Haven and Arwa made her read the announcements at school. The letter was mostly about a camping trip, but the last part said: I read that a 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light. Isn't that something? Eighty percent of us. We stood in a field and there it was, like a spilled bag of sugar across the sky. Haven slept through the whole thing.

"That's us," Chloe said. "The eighty percent. I've never seen it." She thought of last spring, when she'd told Arwa the night sky was boring, just the same five dots every night, and Arwa had looked at her like she'd said books were boring. Chloe had laughed it off then. Now, holding the letter, she wasn't sure she wanted to be the kind of person who laughed things off.

"Whole street's dark," Grandma said. "Might as well test it." They stepped onto the porch in their socks, and Chloe looked up and stopped breathing for a second. There were not five stars. There were hundreds, and across the middle of the sky ran a pale, grainy river of them, exactly like spilled sugar. Somewhere down the block a dog barked twice and quit. Chloe's socks were getting damp from the porch boards, and she didn't care.

Tomorrow she would tell Haven, whose own mother had written that letter and never mentioned it once in six years of carpool. Arwa might ridicule her for taking so long to look up, and Chloe decided she could live with that. "I'm going to draw it before the lights come back," she said, defiant against the whole idea of ordinary skies, and she went inside to find paper.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
The bus let them off in front of the museum just as the doors opened, and Jackson was third in line, right behind Leyla and Ryland. Ms. Demir counted heads twice, then passed out the clipboards. The assignment was to sketch three objects, but Jackson kept getting distracted by small silver boxes tucked into the corners of the display cases, each one with a dial and a thin needle.

"It's a humidity gauge," the guide said when Leyla pointed at one and asked what it was. Then she moved on toward the marble statues, her voice transmitting down the gallery in a flat echo.

Jackson stayed behind. The gauge in the case with an old wooden violin read fifty-one, and the needle was steady. At lunch, in the courtyard, he turned his clipboard over and wrote what he knew. Museums controlled the temperature and humidity. That part was obvious, or the gauges wouldn't be there. But why?

He looked at the questions through the lens of the violin itself. Wood, paper, canvas. He pressed his thumbnail into his sandwich bread and watched the dent stay. Soft things soaked up damp air; dry things gave it back. His own bedroom door stuck shut every August and swung free in January, because the wood swelled and shrank with the weather. If the whole violin swelled and shrank, over and over, the seams would pull, and eventually something would crack or warp. That was the whole reason for the gauges.

Back inside, testing the idea, he stood by the tall window near the instrument cases. He pressed his palm to the glass; it was warm, and outside the sun beat down. A delivery door at the end of the hall stood propped open, and he could feel the outdoor air sliding across the floor, humid and heavy, straight toward the violin case. The gauge's needle had crept up to fifty-four.

Jackson found Ms. Demir by the coatroom. "The delivery door's open near the instruments," he said. "I think it's changing the humidity."

She looked at him for a second, then walked down the hall and pulled the door shut herself. Jackson went back to the case. The needle stood still, and behind the glass the violin lay indifferent to all of it, strings quiet, wood safe in its steady air.

Leyla leaned over his shoulder. "You didn't sketch anything yet."

"I sketched a gauge," Jackson said, and turned his clipboard around to show her.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Joseph stood on the porch of the Tanaka family's house holding a box of almond cookies, and he could not stop staring at the floor. It was his cousin's engagement party, and the whole extended family had been invited, which meant Joseph knew almost nobody except his aunt and uncle. The entryway was lower than the rest of the house, a shallow trench of wooden flooring with a whole row of shoes lined up along one edge, toes pointing toward the door. Two pairs of slippers sat waiting on the higher step like they were expecting somebody.

He was still deciding what to do when a girl his age came up behind him with her mother. Without hesitating, she stepped out of her sneakers, set them neatly beside the others, and slid her feet into slippers. Joseph copied her, feeling clumsy, and kept one hand on the doorframe for balance. His dress shoes looked wrong there, tipped over on their side, so he knelt and straightened them to match the row.

"You must be Joseph," the girl said. "I'm Lorelai. Our moms are cousins." She glanced at his cookies. "Those are for the table? My grandpa calls the entryway the genkan. Everybody's shoes live there."

Joseph wanted to ask a dozen things, starting with how anybody remembered all these rules, but he held back and watched instead. At the doorway to the kitchen he noticed a second, smaller pile of footwear, bathroom slippers lined up by themselves, and a boy he recognized from school, King, stepping out of one pair and into another like changing lanes. Was every room in this house its own small country with its own border crossing? He began to classify the shoes by room: hard slippers for the hallway, rubber ones for the bathroom, socks everywhere else.

Dinner was long and wonderful and full of traps. At home Joseph's family passed plates with reaching forks and elbows everywhere; here each dish arrived with a small ceremony, offered with two hands, received with two hands. When he gave his grandmother's gift, the almond cookies, Lorelai's grandfather accepted it with both palms and a slight bow, then set it, unopened, on a shelf near the door. Joseph felt a flicker of worry. Had he chosen badly? But King had brought a wrapped package too, and it also sat unopened, and Lorelai's mother's gift from yesterday was still sitting there in its paper. A pattern, Joseph thought. Not rejection. Patience.

The only real crisis came when Joseph wandered toward the back hallway in his socks, chasing the smell of grilled fish, and Lorelai's grandmother gasped and waved him back. He looked down and saw it: his socked feet had crossed onto the tatami room's raised edge, where another pair of slippers waited, and a fresh set of shoes sat by the back door as if someone had just gone into the garden. It seemed almost paradox to him that a house so full of rules never once scolded him; people just pointed, smiled, and moved him along like a chess piece.

At the end of the night, he found his own shoes exactly where he had left them, toes pointing out, ready for the road. He stepped down into the genkan, pushed his feet in, and heard Lorelai laugh behind him.

"First time?" she asked.

"Is it that obvious?"

"You bowed to your own shoes," she said.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
story:
Emma stood at the baseline of the gym with nineteen other kids, all of them waiting for the tryouts to start. Ms. Martínez held a clipboard and a speaker that would do the judging today. "First we run the beep test," she announced. "Back and forth between the cones, twenty meters apart. You have to reach the line before each beep." Emma glanced down the court. The cones at each end looked small and far away, like punctuation marks on a very long sentence.

"Twenty meters is the full width of the court plus a bit more," whispered Bianca, who was beside her, stretching her hamstrings. "I've done this at my old school." Emma nodded, but her mind had already gone somewhere else. A math problem. If the beeps came at a steady pace, she could sprint the first few and rest later. But what if the beeps didn't stay steady? She raised her hand. "Ms. Martínez, does the time between beeps change?" Ms. Martínez smiled like someone who enjoyed that question. "Listen for yourself."
