The first level began, and the beeps came slow and lazy, almost polite. Emma trotted, touched the line, trotted back. On the second level the beeps were quicker. On the third, quicker again. So that was the pattern: each new level meant less time to cover the same twenty meters. It was like an algorithm, she thought, one that kept tightening its rules every round. Her original plan, sprint early and coast later, suddenly looked like a bad idea. If she burned everything now, the later levels would eat her alive.

She changed her mind mid-stride. Instead of dashing to the line with seconds to spare, she timed her steps to arrive just before each beep, saving every scrap of energy. Beside her, Raven was sprinting hard and arriving five seconds early every time, then standing still, then sprinting again. "You're going to tire out," Emma panted as they passed. "You have to be fast later, not just now." Raven gave her an acute, skeptical look, the kind that said prove it.

Level six arrived and the beeps snapped at their heels like a small angry dog. Raven, whose legs had turned heavy, missed two beeps in a row and was told to step out. Emma kept her rhythm, arriving with barely a breath to spare, over and over, until the gym blurred and her lungs burned. At level eight, three runners were left. At level eight's final lap, Emma missed by one step and Ms. Martínez blew the whistle.

She bent over, hands on her knees, gulping air. Bianca had also made it through level eight, and the two of them stood together as Ms. Martínez read the list of names for the second round of tryouts. Emma heard her own name and something in her chest jumped higher than she ever had. "Tomorrow," Ms. Martínez said, checking her watch, "we scrimmage at four sharp. Anyone late sits the first half." Emma grinned at Bianca. "Want to petition her for a practice court tonight?" Bianca was already bouncing a ball. "Race you to the outdoor hoops."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel out.
story:
Natalie sorted the tray of small balls at her lab station while Scarlette pushed the foam base across the counter. Ms. Visser had assigned each pair of students an element, and theirs was carbon. The instructions said to place the protons, neutrons and electrons in the right positions, with protons and neutrons clustered in the middle and electrons in rings around them.

"Tucker says the middle doesn't matter as long as it looks good," Scarlette said, gluing the nucleus together.

"That's the conventional way people draw it in cartoons, but Ms. Visser wants the counts right," Natalie said. She counted six red balls into the nucleus. "Six protons."

They added six grey neutrons, then Scarlette handed her the bag of blue electrons. Natalie stuck four onto the wire rings before the bag ran out.

At the next station, Tucker leaned over. "Ours is oxygen. Eight of everything." He studied their model and frowned. "You've only got four electrons. Did you lose some?"

Natalie checked the floor under the counter. Nothing. "Maybe Ms. Visser just gave us fewer."

"Then it should balance," Tucker said. "Four is even, six is even."

Natalie looked at the model again. The red protons were marked with plus signs and the blue electrons with minus signs, the way the diagram on the board showed them. She pulled the diagram closer and counted the symbols in the carbon box.

"Protons are positive and electrons are negative," she said slowly. "A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the charges cancel out."

"So ours doesn't cancel," Scarlette said. "Ours is off by two."

"I was wrong about it balancing," Tucker said. He got up and walked to the supply cabinet.

Ms. Visser came over while Scarlette was threading the fifth blue ball onto the outer ring. "Missing pieces?" she asked.

"The tray was short," Natalie said. "We counted."

Ms. Visser opened the cabinet and shook a fresh bag of electrons into Natalie's palm. Natalie threaded the last one on, counted six and six, and set the finished carbon model beside the diagram, charges matched.

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate, and three tiny bones in the middle ear, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibration to the inner ear.
story:
Eve pressed her ear against the long metal trough of water just as Alejandro tapped a tuning fork against the counter. The hum arrived almost instantly, sharp and quick, like someone plucking a wire inside her head. When she lifted her head and he tapped the fork again in the open air, the sound seemed to dawdle on its way to her, softer and slower, though she knew it had only crossed the same distance.

"Did you hear that?" she asked. "It got to me faster through the water."

Sawer frowned. "Sound can't be faster in water. Water's heavier. Heavy things slow you down, like running through a pool."

"That's your legs," Eve said. "Sound isn't legs."

Ms. Bianchi, who was stacking trays at the back of the lab, raised an eyebrow but said nothing. She had a rule for the afternoons when the three of them stayed late: she would hand out equipment and answer questions with only "yes," "no," or "test it." Eve suspected this was her way of making them isolate the real question from all the guessing.

Eve's question was simple now. If sound reached her ear faster or slower depending on what it traveled through, what happened once it got there? She could not see inside her own ear. "There has to be something in there that catches it," she said. "Like a drum catching a stick."

Alejandro dragged the rolling cart closer. On it sat the model Ms. Bianchi had borrowed from the museum, an ear built giant-sized, its outer curve taller than Eve. Alejandro swung open a panel on its side so they could see within. There was a thin stretched sheet, and behind it three little bones in a row.

"That flat part," Sawyer said, tracing it with a finger, "has to be the eardrum. Sound hits it and it shakes."

Eve touched the first small bone. "Then these pass the shaking along, deeper inside." She tapped the sheet gently with a pencil eraser and all three bones wobbled, one after another, quick as a chain of dominoes. "It's like the vibration hops across them." She pointed at each in turn. "That one looks like a hammer. That one's flat like an anvil, and that last one is shaped like a stirrup."

"So the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup," Alejandro said slowly, as if filing the names somewhere safe.

The door opened and a parent arrived to pick up Sawyer, but Sawyer lingered, holding a paper cup of water to one ear while Alejandro hummed at the other end of the table. In the corner the radiator ticked in the dry, arid air of the overheated lab, and Eve thought the tick sounded fainter than it should.

"Here's what I think," she said. "Sound is just shaking. And the molecules in water are packed closer together than in air, so the shaking gets passed along faster, the way these three bones pass it along. The drum can't do the work alone. It needs things touching it."

Ms. Bianchi, gathering her keys, paused on her way out. "Ambassador of the science fair," she said, dropping a sign-up sheet on the bench beside the model ear, "should probably demonstrate that with the fork and the trough."

Eve picked up the tuning fork and struck it once, hard, against the counter.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users.
story:
The library's computer room smelled like pencil shavings and old carpet, and Maeva had exactly one hour before it closed. Tomorrow her class would debate whether an ad disguised as a search result was fair, and Mr. Chukwu had put her on the "not fair" side. The problem was that she didn't yet know what she was talking about.

"Try searching hummingbirds," suggested Joseph, leaning over from the next computer. "You like hummingbirds." Maeva typed hummingbird food recipe, and a list of links appeared. The first one had a tiny pale box in the corner with the word Ad inside it. She had never noticed that box before, not once, and now she couldn't stop seeing it.

"There are two kinds of results," Kian said from across the table, squinting at her screen. "The ones the search engine finds on its own, and the ones somebody paid to put there." He was supposed to argue the "fair" side tomorrow, and he grinned at her like he already knew he'd win. Maeva scrolled down and clicked the first non-ad result, a site about nectar mixes for hummingbird feeders, because the ad at the top had the same recipe but with a whole online store attached. Something about that felt sneaky, though she couldn't have said why yet.

Then she tried a test. She searched cheap flammable cabinet paint, and then safe cabinet paint, and compared where the paid links showed up. They always sat at the top, dressed up to look like the real results, like a costume. If the Ad labels were small enough, a person in a hurry would click the paid one without ever knowing. Her stomach did a small flip. That was the hidden pattern, and she had found it herself, at a library computer, with forty minutes left on the clock.

She typed federal trade commission search engines into the search box, adding each word carefully the way she'd been practicing, narrowing instead of widening. The result she wanted sat third on the page, no Ad box on it at all. And there it was: in 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users. She read it twice. "It's actually a rule," she said out loud. "Natural results. That's what they call the real ones."

Kian came around the table and read over her shoulder, and his grin faded into something more thoughtful. "Huh," he said. "Maybe I should switch sides." Before the room closed, Maeva grabbed a scrap paper from the front desk and wrote him a note: "Trade you. You take not fair, I'll argue fair, since the rule makes them label the ads. Meet at the playground at nine if you agree." She slid it across the table, and Kian read it, laughed once, and turned the paper over to write back. "Deal," his reply said, "but you're buying the popsicles."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A quotation used as evidence must be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks.
story:
Adam slid his library copy of "The Bridge to Terabithia" across the table and hoped nobody would call on him first. Mr. Toussaint had written one question on the board before book club started: What is this book really about, and can you prove it? Adam knew what the book was about on the surface, a creek, a rope, two kids, but the underneath part, the theme, kept hiding from him like a fish under a rock.

Kaylin went first. "I think it's about how friendship changes you," she said, "and Jess changes because Leslie teaches him imagination." She read her quotation from a sticky note: "She had made him leave his old self behind." Josue frowned at his own copy and turned pages, hunting.

Adam remembered, suddenly, a rainy afternoon last fall when he had tried to fix his grandfather's old radio. He had pulled the back off, thinking he could just dismantle it and see what was wrong, and instead he had found a jumble of parts that meant nothing until his grandfather pointed at one small wire. You don't understand a thing by taking it apart, his grandfather had said. You understand it by noticing what everything has in common. Maybe a theme worked like that. Adam flipped through the book, not looking for one perfect sentence but for a pattern, and he kept finding the same thing: Jess running, drawing, building, pretending. Leslie gave him permission to imagine. He raised his hand. "I think the theme is that imagination makes even an ordinary life fertile, like it can grow things that weren't there before. Like Jess's art." He quoted from memory: "It was up to him to pay back to the world in beauty and caring what Leslie had loaned him in vision and courage."

Mr. Toussaint tilted his head. "Close. Check the page."

Adam found the page, and his stomach dropped. Two words were wrong. The real line said "for beauty and caring," not "to the world in beauty and caring," and it said "in the beauty" somewhere he hadn't remembered at all. "I got some of it wrong," he admitted.

"Then it's not evidence yet," Mr. Toussaint said, sliding a pencil toward him. "It has to be copied word for word, same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks."

Adam copied it carefully, letter by letter, checking twice, and even Josue leaned over to verify the quotation marks. At the end of the meeting, Kaylin passed him a folded note: "Yours was the best motive for our next book. Co-present with me Tuesday?" He read it twice, wrote "Deal" underneath, and handed it back on her way out the door.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In "divide and choose," one person splits something into two parts and the other picks first, so the divider has a reason to make the parts equal.
story:
The storm knocked the power out at Lya's house just after six, and the three of them, Hazel, Lya, and Charles-Antoine, were left in the half-dark living room with a board game half set up and nothing else to do. Lya's father went out to the shed and came back saying the generator would run the fridge and one lamp, so they dragged the game to the kitchen table under the lamp's cone of light.

Then they found the problem. The game needed exactly two territories dealt out for the starting hand, and there was one packet of cards that had already been opened. Lya and Charles-Antoine each grabbed for it at the same time. Charles-Antoine said he was the guest. Lya said it was her house. The mood around the table turned volatile fast, and Hazel could see the whole evening going with it if she didn't salvage the game now.

She thought about her two cousins at a birthday party last spring, screaming over the last piece of cake until her grandmother stepped in. Grandma hadn't just cut the cake. She had made one cousin cut it and let the other cousin pick first, and the screaming stopped, because the cutter suddenly wanted both pieces to be exactly the same. Hazel hadn't understood it at the time, but now, watching Lya and Charles-Antoine glare at each other, she worked out the pattern: the person dividing has a reason to make the parts equal, because the other person picks first.

"Okay," Hazel said. "Charles-Antoine, you split the cards into two groups. Lya picks which group she wants first." Charles-Antoine frowned, then shuffled the packet and laid out two piles, counting each card twice. Lya studied both piles, took one, and pushed the rest across the table.

Charles-Antoine flipped through his pile. "These are actually even," he said, sounding almost disappointed.

"Set them down, it's your move," Lya said, and she shook the dice in her fist.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
The trumpet in Jeremy's case felt heavier every Thursday, and he knew why. He'd practice for two whole hours on Wednesday night, his lips aching, and then walk into the community center band room and flub the same three notes in front of Sami and Atticus.

"Again?" Sami said, not meanly, just surprised.

"I practiced forever," Jeremy said. "My cheeks practically fell off."

Ms. López tapped the music stand. "From the top, everybody."

That night Jeremy flopped on his bed and stared at the ceiling. Something didn't add up. Last summer he'd tried to teach himself to juggle by throwing balls for one marathon Saturday, and he'd ended up chasing oranges all over the kitchen. Then he'd juggled for just five minutes every day after breakfast, and by August he could do it without thinking. Was the trumpet like that? He couldn't see inside his own brain to check, but maybe he could run a test.

So he spread his practice out. Ten minutes Monday, ten Tuesday, ten Wednesday, small bites instead of one giant meal. He wrote the times on a sticky note so he'd know if his intuition about the plan was right.

Thursday came. He lifted the horn, and the notes came out clean, one after another, like water from a tap.

"There it is!" Atticus shouted from the second row.

Sami leaned over. "What did you do different?"

"Short practices, every day," Jeremy said. "Same total time, just spread out. One big night of practice doesn't stick the same way."

"Wait," Sami said. "I cram every Wednesday too."

Ms. López smiled and raised her baton. "Then this is going to be an interesting month."

Jeremy raised the trumpet to his lips and thought, with a small thrill, that even his fancy new routine was really just one simple trick. "Count us in," he said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Lauren stood at the picnic table in the backyard, cracking eggs into a bowl while her father lit the grill. Tonight was her turn to cook, and she had appointed herself head chef of the pancakes, a decision she was starting to regret. Her little brother, Evan, sat on the porch steps with a clipboard, because he had decided the pancakes needed judging, and fairness was his one criterion: five points if they tasted good, zero if they tasted like soap.

The first batch came out flat and strangely bitter. Evan took one bite, made a face like a deflating balloon, and wrote a large zero. "This," he announced, "is the worst contemporary cuisine I have ever reviewed."

"Thanks, Evan."

Lauren looked at the little box she had used instead of baking powder, because the baking powder tin was empty and she'd figured the two were basically the same thing. Clearly they were not. She flipped the pancake over and studied it, thinking. The muffins she made last month had baking soda in them, but that recipe also had buttermilk, which was sour. This pancake recipe had no buttermilk, no lemon juice, nothing sour at all. She turned the empty tin over and read the ingredient list on the paper label she had peeled off earlier. Then she called Adelyn, who baked constantly.

"Baking powder is different," Adelyn said. "Baking powder already has baking soda and a dry acid in it, so it works even when the recipe has nothing sour."

Lauren hung up and stared at the bowl. So the acid had to come from somewhere. She couldn't see it or taste it, but the pancake recipe got its rise from that hidden partnership inside the powder. Since she only had plain baking soda, she would have to supply the acid herself. She stirred in a spoonful of lemon juice, watched the batter fizz and puff up like something alive, and ladled it onto the griddle.

The second pancakes rose into golden rounds. Evan circled the table twice, tasted, and held up his clipboard with a shaky five written on it, plus a star he drew on afterward.

"I'm still the judge," he said, reaching for a third pancake.

fact: According to the American Academy of Dermatology, about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne.
story:
The pharmacy smelled like mint and cough drops, and Alyssa stood in the deodorant aisle feeling like a spy on her first mission. Her mom had given her ten dollars and one instruction: pick something, because "your armpits have opinions now." She grabbed a purple stick labeled "fresh rain" and pretended she was sophisticated enough to know what fresh rain was supposed to smell like. Rain smelled like wet sidewalk, in her expert opinion.

Then she heard a familiar groan from the next aisle. Linden was staring at a mirror display, pressing one finger against the three red spots on his chin like he was trying to push them back in.

"It's over," he said. "My face is ruined. I'm the villain of the seventh grade now."

"You're not the antagonist of anything," Alyssa said. "You're the antagonist of one mirror." She came around the shelf and looked at the acne section, which was enormous, wall after wall of creams and washes and tiny stickers you put on spots overnight. That gave her an idea. If acne were rare, why would there be enough products to fill a whole wall?

She turned the nearest box over and found a fact printed on the back, and she read it out loud. "It says here that about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne."

Linden lowered his finger. "Eighty-five? Out of a hundred?"

"Out of a hundred. So in any classroom, look around and most people either have it or will."

"That's basically everyone," Linden said. "Genevieve's going to get it too. And Marcus. Even the principal, if he's under 24." He grinned, then checked himself. "Wait, how old is the principal?"

"No idea, but I'm not asking." Alyssa held up her purple deodorant. "Also, we apparently smell now, so I'm buying this."

"Get me one too," Linden said. "The manliest fresh rain they have."

fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
The community centre camp split into two teams on Monday morning by drawing names from a plastic tub. Ariana drew a red card, so she was on the Red team, and her best friend Daria drew blue and stood across the gym with the others. By Wednesday, the Red team chanted whenever they beat Blue at floor hockey, and Josie, who was on Blue, refused to sit with Ariana at lunch. "It's just a game," Ariana said, and Josie said, "You're on Red, you wouldn't get it."

Ariana thought about that all through swim time. The teams had not been chosen for skill or friendship or anything at all. The cards came out of a tub at random. So why did everyone act like the tub meant something? On Thursday she devised a test. She cut thirty paper squares, wrote A on fifteen and B on fifteen, folded them, and dropped them in an empty tennis ball can. Then she walked the waiting room outside the gym and asked kids to draw one and pin it to their shirts.

Within an hour, the A kids had claimed the good couch by the vending machine and were telling B kids it was full, even when it wasn't. Nobody had said the teams were for anything. Ariana watched a boy named only in her head as Tall Kid grab his square, see the B, and sigh like he'd lost something. Two girls who came in together drew different letters and ended up on opposite sides of the room by choice.

She looked it up later in the community centre's small library, where a shelf held Mr. Lau's old psychology books. One chapter described experiments by a psychologist named Henri Tajfel. People favoured their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Ariana read it twice, then copied it onto the back of a red card.

On Friday she left the tennis ball can on the lunch table with a sign that said "Pick a letter." Josie read the sign, drew a card, and looked at the B. Ariana held up her own card, which she had not drawn from anything, and flipped it over to show the copied sentence. Josie read it, then slid her tray around the corner of the table and said, "Sit down, Red."
